newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Mars rover set for launch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Mars rover set for launch.

text.p: A U.S. Mars probe carrying the first rover designed to explore the rocky Martian surface was set for blastoff early on Tuesday, NASA said.
The Mars Pathfinder, NASA's second probe destined for the Red Planet this year, was to begin its 310-million-mile journey at 2:03 a.m. EST (0703 GMT) riding atop a McDonnell Douglas Delta 2 rocket.
The blastoff had been delayed 24 hours by dismal weather associated with a cold front that passed through central Florida. Perfect weather was forecast for Tuesday.

The probe will follow NASA's Mars Global Surveyor on the path to the Red Planet but will take a faster, more direct route. Pathfinder is expected to overtake Surveyor, launched on Nov. 7, and arrive at Mars next July 4.

Pathfinder, developed at a cost of $150 million, carries a landing station and the first rover designed to explore the Martian surface. The six-wheeled vehicle, called Sojourner, will explore the landing site, beaming back pictures and using an "electronic nose" to sniff out the composition of rocks.
"You can think about the rover, which is about the size of your laser printer, as a little two-foot geologist," said Matthew Golombek, the project scientist.

The rover will be operated by remote control from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California. Drivers will use virtual reality goggles linked to cameras on the lander and the rover to guide the vehicle across the rock-strewn surface.

Pathfinder is targeted to land on a plain in Mars' northern hemisphere, thought to be the site of great floods when water flowed on the planet millions of years ago. The 1,256-lb (570 kg) probe will plunge directly into the thin Martian atmosphere, protected by a bowl-shaped heat shield.

When it has braked to nearly twice the speed of sound a parachute will open to slow its descent further. Pathfinder will bounce about 40 feet (12 metres) high as it hits the Martian surface, the impact cushioned by 24 air bags, each 3.3 feet (one metre) in diameter. It may take a dozen bounces before the craft comes to rest.
The sides of the pyramid-shaped craft will open like flower petals, revealing the lander's mini-Martian weather station and freeing the Sojourner rover.

During Pathfinder's month-long mission on the surface, images and Martian weather reports will be posted on the internet daily, NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin said. "There will be a virtual presence on Mars so everybody in America, and for that matter around the world, can participate."
